s: Hasbro DEF 14A filed 4 Apr 2025 (beneficial ownership table); Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026; age from Hasbro DEF 14A 2 Apr 2019
m: 5,023,585 Hasbro shares held in trusts for his benefit plus 4,619 held directly, times the 93.54 dollar close on 21 Aug 2026, is 470 million dollars; excludes about 2.16m shares in Hassenfeld Family Initiatives LLC and 223,191 in the family foundation; he fell below the 5 percent line by Mar 2026, so haircut
did: Third-generation head of the Pawtucket toy company his grandfather founded in 1923; ran Hasbro as chief executive from 1989 to 2003 and chairman to 2008, buying Tonka in 1991 and Galoob in 1998 and locking up the Star Wars and Pokemon licences, taking revenue past 3 billion dollars.
why: Hasbro's value sat in evergreen brands plus licensed film properties, and he bet the balance sheet on licences at the moment cinema became a toy channel - the 1997 Star Wars and 1999 Pokemon deals - while buying Tonka and Galoob so Mattel could not consolidate the second tier.
obst: He took the chief executive job in 1989 only because his elder brother Stephen died at 47, then fought off Mattel's 1996 merger approach and absorbed heavy losses when the 1999 Pokemon and Star Wars programmes over-shipped retail and had to be written down.
turn: Rejecting Mattel's roughly 5.2 billion dollar merger approach in early 1996, which kept Hasbro independent and family-influenced instead of folding it into its only global rival.

s: BETA Technologies DEF 14A filed 29 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 14 Apr 2026); NYSE close 21 Aug 2026
m: 16,569,253 shares beneficially owned - 8,067,769 Class A including exercisable options and vested PSUs, plus all 8,501,484 Class B - times the 24.74 dollar BETA close on 21 Aug 2026, is 410 million dollars
did: Founded BETA Technologies on the South Burlington airport in 2017 after United Therapeutics chief Martine Rothblatt asked for an electric aircraft that could move manufactured organs; built the ALIA CX300 and A250, a national charging network, and listed BETA on the NYSE in November 2025.
why: He chased certification and revenue instead of the eVTOL hype cycle: BETA flew a conventional-takeoff electric plane first, sold chargers to airports and to rivals, and took strategic money from GE Aerospace and Amazon, so it had FAA progress and cash while competitors were still on prototypes.
obst: Vermont had no aerospace supply chain, so motors, batteries, inverters and flight software had to be built in-house on an airport lot, and the FAA had no certification basis for the aircraft category he was asking it to approve.
turn: Rothblatt's 2017 order for an organ-delivery aircraft, which turned a garage electric-motor project into a funded programme with a named launch customer before any eVTOL company had revenue.

s: Planet Fitness Form 4 filings, Oct 2016 to Jan 2024 (SEC EDGAR, CIK 1649552); age from Planet Fitness DEF 14A filed 22 Mar 2023
m: 267 open-market sale lines across his Form 4s from Oct 2016 to Dec 2023 total 300.6 million dollars gross; New Hampshire taxes no capital gains, so federal tax near 24 percent leaves about 229 million dollars, before 2012 recapitalisation proceeds and a decade of reinvestment
did: Joined the first Planet Fitness in Dover, New Hampshire in 1993 as a front-desk clerk, became an owner alongside founders Michael and Marc Grondahl, built the 10-dollar-a-month Judgement Free Zone format, and ran the chain as chief executive from 2013 to September 2023, reaching about 2,500 clubs.
why: He priced a gym below a monthly cable bill and made the economics work on members who never show up: high-volume, low-staff clubs with no trainers, no classes and no daycare, funded by franchisees who were also required to buy their equipment packages from the parent company.
obst: Covid closed every club in March 2020 and erased membership revenue for months at a company whose whole model is monthly dues; before that he had to convert a family-run gym partnership into a disciplined franchisor after selling control to TSG Consumer Partners in 2012.
turn: The 2003 switch to a 10-dollar monthly price in a purple-and-yellow, cardio-machine-only club, which turned a local New Hampshire gym chain into a franchise system.

s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2023 - 300 million dollars, listed at Stowe, Vermont, age 59
m: Published Forbes list figure of 300 million dollars from the June 2023 ranking, carried forward; Burton stays wholly owned by Carpenter and her three sons and she has not been re-listed since Forbes cut the list to billionaires
did: Joined the snowboard company her husband Jake Burton Carpenter had started in a Vermont barn, took over its books and its European expansion from 1983, became chief executive in 2015, and inherited full ownership when he died of cancer in November 2019; Burton holds roughly a third of the global market.
why: Burton controlled the sport rather than just selling into it: the Carpenters funded the global rider team, lobbied ski resorts to lift snowboard bans through the late 1980s, and kept the company private so it could carry inventory through warm winters that killed venture-funded rivals.
obst: Snowboarding nearly failed as a business twice - resorts banned boards into the early 1990s, and participation fell after 2010 - and she ran the company through her husband's testicular cancer and later Miller Fisher syndrome before his death in 2019.
turn: Jake Burton Carpenter's death in November 2019, which left her sole owner and chair of a company she had already co-run for 36 years.

s: Schedule 13G/A filed 13 Feb 2017 (holdings as of 31 Dec 2016); Form 4 filings 2016-17; NYSE close 21 Aug 2026; age from Planet Fitness DEF 14A 5 Apr 2016
m: Last SEC-disclosed position was 5,067,317 Planet Fitness Holdings units and Class B shares, 7.7 percent, at 31 Dec 2016; nothing filed since, so that block at the 54.20 dollar close on 21 Aug 2026 is 275 million dollars, cut back for probable post-2017 selling and tax, plus 20.3 million dollars of Form 4 sales
did: Co-founded Planet Fitness with his brother Michael in Dover, New Hampshire in 1992 after the pair took over a failing Golds Gym franchise, served as chief financial officer from 1998, and sold control to TSG Consumer Partners in 2012 three years before the company listed.
why: The brothers worked out that the profitable gym member is the one who never comes, so they stripped out trainers, classes and free weights, filled 20,000 square feet with cardio machines, and sold franchises whose equipment packages they also supplied - a royalty stream plus a hardware margin.
obst: They inherited a money-losing Golds Gym franchise in Dover in 1992 and had to persuade a landlord and equipment lenders to back a format nobody had seen; national franchise growth then had to be funded from cash flow because banks would not lend against 10-dollar memberships.
turn: The November 2012 recapitalisation in which TSG Consumer Partners bought control, converting the brothers' operating stake into cash plus a minority holding that survived into the 2015 IPO.

s: IDEXX Laboratories DEF 14A filed 27 Mar 2026 (ownership and age as of 8-27 Mar 2026); Form 4 filings 2012-2026; Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 83,803 IDXX shares at the 556.93 dollar close on 21 Aug 2026 is 46.7 million dollars; 238,917 options exercisable within 60 days at strikes from 141.60 to 459.76 dollars carry roughly 54 million dollars of intrinsic value; plus 79.6 million dollars of gross Form 4 sales taxed near 31 percent
did: Joined IDEXX in 2012 to run companion-animal diagnostics, became chief executive in 2019 and executive chair in 2026, and grew the Westbrook, Maine veterinary diagnostics maker past 4.3 billion dollars of revenue by placing in-clinic analysers and selling the consumables that only fit them.
why: IDEXX sells analysers at thin margin and then owns the clinic's test volume permanently, because the slides and cartridges are proprietary; he accelerated that lock by putting instruments into clinics on multi-year consumable commitments during the pandemic pet boom, when vet visits spiked.
obst: He was handed the job mid-2019 when a long-serving chief executive left abruptly, then had to keep instrument placements moving through Covid clinic closures and a 2022-23 slump in US veterinary visits that cut organic growth to low single digits and halved the share price from its peak.
turn: His June 2019 elevation to interim chief executive, made permanent that November, which put a career diagnostics operator in charge of the razor-and-blade conversion.

s: Casella Waste Systems DEF 14A filed 17 Apr 2026 (ownership and age as of 31 Mar 2026); Form 4 filings 2003-2026; Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,008,526 CWST shares - 514,426 Class A plus 494,100 Class B - times the 92.01 dollar close on 21 Aug 2026 is 92.8 million dollars; add 67.5 million dollars of gross Form 4 open-market sales since 2003, taxed at roughly 30 percent in Vermont, for about 140 million dollars
did: Started hauling trash in Rutland in 1975 with one truck bought after his freshman year at Vermont Technical College, built Casella Waste Systems into a vertically integrated 1.8 billion dollar-a-year Northeast hauler and landfill operator, and took it public on Nasdaq in 1997.
why: Landfill airspace in New England is close to unpermittable, so owning the disposal end let him price collection against competitors who had to pay him to tip; he then bought small family haulers inside the same haul radius and pushed their volume into holes he already owned.
obst: The 1999 collapse in recycled commodity prices plus a badly timed expansion left the company heavily levered; the stock fell under 2 dollars in 2009 and he had to sell the western operations and give ground to a turnaround team before he could buy growth again.
turn: The 2013 repricing of landfill and collection contracts around cost recovery rather than volume, which ended roughly a decade of negative free cash flow and re-rated the stock.

s: Casella Waste Systems DEF 14A filed 17 Apr 2026 (ownership and age as of 31 Mar 2026); Form 4 filings 2003-2026; Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,089,578 CWST shares - 595,478 Class A plus 494,100 Class B - times the 92.01 dollar close on 21 Aug 2026 is 100.2 million dollars; add 43.0 million dollars of gross Form 4 sales since 2003 taxed near 30 percent; excludes privately held Casella Construction, which is not valued here
did: Co-founded Casella Waste Systems with his brother John in Rutland in 1975 and took the landfill construction, closure and heavy-equipment side; he separately owns Casella Construction, which builds and caps the public company's landfills and billed it 8.6 million dollars in 2025.
why: The brothers split the business so the capital-heavy part - cell construction, liners, caps, gas systems - sat with an owner-operator of the machines; that kept landfill development inside the family and gave Casella permitting and build speed that regional rivals hiring contractors could not match.
obst: Related-party contracting between his private Casella Construction and the listed company drew repeated governance scrutiny, and every award above 500,000 dollars has had to clear a competitive bid process approved by independent directors.
turn: The 1997 IPO, which turned a family hauling partnership into ten-vote Class B stock that let the two brothers keep control of the company while raising outside landfill capital.

s: IPG Photonics DEF 14A filed 1 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 20 Mar 2026) and 10-K filed 23 Feb 2026 for age; Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 963,922 IPGP shares beneficially owned jointly with his spouse and IPG director Natalia Pavlova, plus an 8 percent economic interest in IP Fibre Devices UK Ltd which holds 6,529,002 shares, or 522,320 shares, gives 1,486,242 shares times the 73.26 dollar close on 21 Aug 2026, about 109 million dollars
did: Named by IPG as a co-founder of the fibre-laser maker started in 1990 by Valentin Gapontsev; he led its laser engineering, serving as deputy general manager of its main foreign subsidiary from 2005, chief technology officer from 2011 to 2022 and chief scientist since, from IPG's Massachusetts plants.
why: IPG made its own pump diodes, fibre and combiners rather than buying them, so it could drop prices roughly a tenth a year and still hold gross margins above 50 percent; rivals purchasing diodes on the open market could not follow that curve into automotive and shipyard cutting.
obst: Much of IPG's engineering and diode production sat in Russia, and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine forced the company to write down and unwind those operations; at the same time Chinese makers led by Raycus took the low-power market on price.
turn: The early-2000s pivot from telecom amplifiers to kilowatt industrial cutting lasers, which found a market that survived the telecom bust that killed most fibre-optics companies.
